introLesson.title: Introduction to Frankenstein

sections.authorBiography: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on 30 August 1797, the daughter of two of the most famous radical writers of the 1790s: the philosopher William Godwin (author of Political Justice) and the feminist Mary Wollstonecraft (author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman). Wollstonecraft died of puerperal fever about eleven days after the birth, so Mary grew up with her mother's books rather than her mother. In 1814, at sixteen, she left England with the married poet Percy Bysshe Shelley; they married in December 1816, weeks after his first wife's suicide. She began Frankenstein at eighteen and published it at twenty. Her adult life was marked by loss: three of her four children died young, and Percy drowned in Italy in July 1822. She supported herself and her surviving son by writing, produced novels including The Last Man (1826), edited Percy's poems, and died in London on 1 February 1851.
sections.historicalContext: The novel was born in the summer of 1816, the "year without a summer," when ash from the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia chilled and darkened Europe. Mary, Percy, her stepsister Claire Clairmont, Lord Byron and Byron's physician John Polidori were kept indoors near Lake Geneva, and Byron proposed that each write a ghost story. The science in the air was electricity and life: Luigi Galvani had made dissected frogs' legs twitch with current, and in 1803 his nephew Giovanni Aldini publicly applied current to the corpse of an executed man in London. The book also belongs to Romanticism, a movement that prized feeling, nature and the solitary genius, and that was fascinated by Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for humankind and was punished for it; the novel's subtitle is The Modern Prometheus. Behind it, too, is Mary's inheritance from her parents' arguments about education, injustice and how society makes people what they are.

publicationAndReception.publication: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously in three volumes on 1 January 1818 (London: Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor and Jones), in an edition of about 500 copies, with a preface by Percy Shelley and a dedication to William Godwin. A second edition (1823), arranged by Godwin, named Mary as author after a stage version, Richard Brinsley Peake's Presumption, became a hit. In 1831 she revised the text heavily for Colburn and Bentley's Standard Novels and added the Introduction that tells the story of its origin; that 1831 text is the one we read.
publicationAndReception.then: Early reviews were split. Walter Scott, in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine (March 1818), praised its "original genius" and assumed Percy Shelley was the author; John Wilson Croker in the Quarterly Review called it "a tissue of horrible and disgusting absurdity." Many reviewers were uneasy with a story that seemed to question God and moral order, and with an anonymous author linked to Godwin's radicals.
publicationAndReception.now: Today Frankenstein is one of the most taught novels in English. Brian Aldiss (Billion Year Spree, 1973) called it the origin of science fiction; feminist critics beginning with Ellen Moers (Literary Women, 1976) read it as a "birth myth" shaped by Mary's experience of pregnancy and infant death; others read it through politics, race, disability and bioethics. Its title has become shorthand in debates about genetic engineering and artificial intelligence, and 2018 brought bicentenary editions and projects worldwide.

sections.overview: A ship's captain, Robert Walton, sailing toward the North Pole, writes letters to his sister. In the ice he rescues a dying stranger, Victor Frankenstein, who tells him how, as a young student, he discovered the secret of life and built a living being. What happens to Victor, his family and his creation is told in three nested voices: Walton's, Victor's and, at the center, the creature's own. The book asks what we owe the things we make and the people we reject.

mainThemes.note: what a maker owes what it makes; watch how often the creature asks to be cared for and how Victor answers.
the hunger to discover, shared by Walton and Victor; ask whether the book condemns curiosity or something more specific.
almost every character is cut off from someone; notice who is allowed to belong and why.
is anyone born a monster, or are monsters made by how they are treated?
mountains, ice and storms that awe and dwarf human beings.

sections.whyItMatters: Frankenstein is the founding story for every argument about technology that outruns responsibility, from gene editing to artificial intelligence, and its creature still speaks for anyone judged by appearance before being heard. It also shows students that a teenager wrote one of the most influential books in the world.

spoilerOverview.text: Victor abandons the creature the moment it wakes. Rejected by every human it meets, the creature kills Victor's brother William (and frames Justine, who is executed), demands a mate, and, when Victor destroys the half-made female, kills Clerval and then Elizabeth on her wedding night. Victor pursues the creature to the Arctic and dies on Walton's ship; the creature mourns him and vanishes into the dark to die.

flags: The exact night of the ghost-story proposal and of Mary's waking dream is uncertain: her 1831 account compresses events, and Polidori's diary points to mid-June 1816. Present the 1831 story as her own later recollection.
The extent of Percy Shelley's edits to the 1818 manuscript is debated (Charles E. Robinson's 2008 edition marks his contributions). He wrote the 1818 Preface; the novel is Mary's.
The first-edition print run is usually given as about 500 copies; treat it as approximate.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together” slowly and put it in my own words: In her 1831 introduction, Shelley describes seeing, eyes closed, a pale student of forbidden arts kneeling beside the thing he had assembled. Next, craft. I notice the creature is called only "the thing he had put together," a phrase that refuses it a name or a human status from the start. The strongest word is “unhallowed”: it means unholy, so the science is framed as a violation of something sacred. Then, effect. What does Shelley's waking vision tell us about the novel she will write? My answer: Shelley presents the novel's seed as a nightmare of a creator who has crossed a forbidden line; the image of maker and made, frightened and unnamed, is the relationship the whole novel examines.

segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): A ship's captain, Robert Walton, sailing toward the North Pole, writes letters to his sister. In the ice he rescues a dying stranger, Victor Frankenstein, who tells him how, as a young student, he discovered the secret of life and built a living being. What happens to Victor, his family and his creation is told in three nested voices: Walton's, Victor's and, at the center, the creature's own. The book asks what we owe the things we make and the people we reject. Themes to track: creation and responsibility: what a maker owes what it makes; watch how often the creature asks to be cared for and how Victor answers. ambition and knowledge: the hunger to discover, shared by Walton and Victor; ask whether the book condemns curiosity or something more specific. isolation and companionship: almost every character is cut off from someone; notice who is allowed to belong and why. nature and nurture: is anyone born a monster, or are monsters made by how they are treated? the sublime: mountains, ice and storms that awe and dwarf human beings.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Shelley began Frankenstein at eighteen, in the summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva, during a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron and Percy Shelley, at a time when scientists were experimenting with electricity on dead bodies. How might that setting and science shape the novel? Answer: Accept answers such as: galvanism made reanimation seem possible; the contest pushed her toward horror; she was surrounded by Romantic poets who prized nature and feeling; she had already lost a baby, which may connect to themes of creation and loss.

introLesson.objective: Students will explain, in a 3-sentence exit ticket, how one fact about Mary Shelley's life or times connects to the costs of unchecked ambition in “Frankenstein”, and will set up a reading journal with a prediction and a question for each of 3 themes (the costs of unchecked ambition, creation and responsibility, isolation and the need for companionship).

criticalVoices.quote: This is a novel, or more properly a romantic fiction, of a nature so peculiar, that we ought to describe the species before attempting any account of the individual production.
criticalVoices.speaker: Walter Scott (attrib.), novelist and critic
criticalVoices.source: "Remarks on Frankenstein, or the Modern Prometheus; A Novel," Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine 2:12 (March 1818), p. 613 (opening sentence)
criticalVoices.useNote: Bell-ringer: Scott could not name the genre in 1818. What would you call it (Gothic, science fiction, philosophical romance)? Defend one label with a detail from the Introduction.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Classify the novel's genre and explain how its structure (frame narrative, "marvellous" premise) shapes meaning.

criticalVoices.quote: Our readers will guess from this summary, what a tissue of horrible and disgusting absurdity this work presents.
criticalVoices.speaker: John Wilson Croker (attrib.; the review is unsigned), critic
criticalVoices.source: Review of Frankenstein, The Quarterly Review 18 (January 1818), 379-385, p. 382
criticalVoices.useNote: Pair with Scott's and Percy Shelley's praise: why did reviewers in 1818 split so sharply? Students sort the three reviews on a moral-vs-aesthetic axis.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Trace the novel's reception at publication ("then") against its reputation today ("now").

lessonPlan.title: Frankenstein unit
lessonPlan.author: Mary Shelley
lessonPlan.editionNote: The reading text is Mary Shelley's revised 1831 edition (Standard Ebooks, from Project Gutenberg #42324), which also prints the 1818 Preface and the 1831 Introduction. In 1818 Elizabeth is Victor's cousin; in 1831 she is the orphaned daughter of a Milanese nobleman, adopted by Victor's mother. Chapter breaks also differ (e.g. around Chapter III). Cite this edition.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Frankenstein.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Frankenstein: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Frankenstein has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to the costs of unchecked ambition.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Frankenstein. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this chapter, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the chapter on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the chapter to the costs of unchecked ambition.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the chapter quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Frankenstein.

essentialQuestions: What does Frankenstein suggest about the costs of unchecked ambition?
What does Frankenstein suggest about creation and responsibility?
What does Frankenstein suggest about isolation and the need for companionship?
What does Frankenstein suggest about nature versus nurture?
What does Frankenstein suggest about the sublime power of nature?
objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the novel in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the chapter quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

items.prompt: Which literary element does this describe in “Introduction”? Shelley speaks in her own voice, thirteen years later, as an author looking back. Which literary element does this describe in “Chapter IV”? Charnel-houses, dissecting rooms, pale cheeks: the work is described as unhealthy and secret.
Which literary element does this describe in “Chapter XI”? Sensory discovery (the moon, birdsong, fire) told with the wonder of a newborn.
Which literary element does this describe in “Chapter XIII”? Learning history and social order, the creature realizes he has no place: no money, family or name.
Which literary element does this describe in “Chapter XVIII”? Clerval, a lover of nature and poetry, contrasts with Victor's misery.

items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “Shelley frames her novel as a creation that, unlike Victor's, is accepted and sent out with care.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive in part. “And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper” (Introduction, paragraph 15) supports it: By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make. But “Invention, it must be humbly admitted, does not consist in creating out of void, but out of chaos” (Introduction, paragraph 9) complicates it: Shelley's theory of creativity: you build from existing materials, as Victor builds from old bones. Good evidence for a claim about the novel's self-awareness, and its “not” marks a limit or reversal the claim passes over. The claim is therefore a strong reading, not a complete one, and a careful answer says where it stops applying.

criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

But “Of what a strange nature is knowledge! It clings to the mind, when it has once seized on it, like a lichen on the rock” (Chapter XIII, paragraph 19) complicates it: Simile for knowledge that cannot be unlearned, and it pulls the other way. Weighing the two passages, the claim survives, but only once it admits the tension the second passage creates.

Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “Shelley frames her novel as a creation that, unlike Victor's, is accepted and sent out with care.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive in part. “And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper” (Introduction, paragraph 15) supports it: By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make. But “Invention, it must be humbly admitted, does not consist in creating out of void, but out of chaos” (Introduction, paragraph 9) complicates it: Shelley's theory of creativity: you build from existing materials, as Victor builds from old bones. Good evidence for a claim about the novel's self-awareness, and its “not” marks a limit or reversal the claim passes over. The claim is therefore a strong reading, not a complete one, and a careful answer says where it stops applying.

Places the book in real time and place; compare with the 1831 Introduction's fuller account. The evidence is “I passed the summer of 1816 in the environs of Geneva” (Preface, paragraph 4). This develops creation and responsibility: The Preface claims the story shows "the amiableness of domestic affection"; keep this phrase on the board. The novel will test it: domestic love is shown, then destroyed. The words “environs” and “passed” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

By calling Walton's desire an "intoxicating draught" and hoping it will not be "a serpent to sting you," Victor links the pursuit of knowledge to addiction and to the biblical Fall, so everything he tells next is offered as a lesson. The evidence is “You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting…” (Letter IV, paragraph 32), which shows the serpent alludes to Eden: knowledge as temptation and fall. Strong for a theme claim. This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor recognizes himself in Walton and warns him; the story becomes a cautionary tale told for a listener's benefit.

Victor treats science as a spirit controlling him, shifting responsibility. The evidence is “Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate” (Chapter II, paragraph 7). This develops ambition and knowledge: the desire to learn "the secrets of heaven and earth" begins as wonder and becomes obsession. The words “philosophy” and “regulated” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

The words “bestowing” and “animation” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

He decides that "nothing in human shape could have destroyed that fair child," so he is certain who did it, yet he lets Justine be accused rather than reveal his secret. Creation and responsibility

He confesses only in riddles ("I am the assassin") and fixates on the creature's threat to himself, so the one person who loves him never learns the danger she is in. The evidence is “I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations” (Chapter XXII, paragraph 6) — Confession to his father, dismissed as madness. Shelley presents herself as a parent of the book. Use this to connect author and character: both make something "hideous," but only one blesses it. The evidence is “And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper” (Introduction, paragraph 15). This develops creation and responsibility: Shelley calls the book her "hideous progeny" and sends it out into the world, as Victor does his creature; but unlike Victor she wishes it to "prosper." The author models the care the character fails to give. The words “progeny” and “prosper” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make.

Dismissal without explanation; Victor later blames this. The evidence is “My dear Victor, do not waste your time upon this; it is sad trash” (Chapter II, paragraph 7). The claim is persuasive in part. “He was soon borne away by the waves, and lost in darkness and distance” (Chapter XXIV, paragraph 75) supports it: Victor advises "seek happiness in tranquillity and avoid ambition" yet adds that another may succeed; the creature disappears into "darkness and distance," leaving judgment open. items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “Victor's secrecy leaves Elizabeth vulnerable.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.
items.expected: The claim is persuasive in part. “I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations” (Chapter XXII, paragraph 6) supports it: He confesses only in riddles ("I am the assassin") and fixates on the creature's threat to himself, so the one person who loves him never learns the danger she is in. But “Do you not love another” (Chapter XXII, paragraph 14) complicates it: the line (Elizabeth's honest question) shows the same issue from another side, and its “not” marks a limit or reversal the claim passes over. A fair verdict is that the claim is mostly right but overstated; it needs a limiting clause to cover that passage.

scoringGuide.full: 4 points: all four criteria met.
scoringGuide.partial: 3: one criterion missing; 2: two missing; 1: a judgment with no usable evidence.
scoringGuide.zero: 0: off-text, restates the claim, or blank.
criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

Isolation through allusion. The evidence is “Like Adam, I was apparently united by no link to any other being in existence” (Chapter XV, paragraph 7). This develops nature and nurture: rejection is based on sight; the blind man alone judges him by his words.
The creature's longing for release.
Introduction
Point of view

An allusion that promises he will not offend against nature; readers who know Coleridge sense danger. The evidence is “I shall kill no albatross” (Letter II, paragraph 6). This develops isolation and companionship: the desire for a sympathetic friend is the thread connecting Walton, Victor and the creature. The words “albatross” and “shall” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

The serpent alludes to Eden: knowledge as temptation and fall. Strong for a theme claim. The evidence is “You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting…” (Letter IV, paragraph 32). This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor recognizes himself in Walton and warns him; the story becomes a cautionary tale told for a listener's benefit. The words “gratification” and “knowledge” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Victor treats science as a spirit controlling him, shifting responsibility. The evidence is “Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate” (Chapter II, paragraph 7). This develops ambition and knowledge: the desire to learn "the secrets of heaven and earth" begins as wonder and becomes obsession. The words “philosophy” and “regulated” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
Foreshadowing
Chapter III

The creature's "hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me," a gesture of need, and Victor simply "escaped"; the word "seemingly" shows he does not know what it wants and does not stay to find out. The evidence is “one hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me, but I escaped” (Chapter V, paragraph 3), which shows the creature's first gesture is reaching; Victor's response is flight. Key evidence that the creature is abandoned before it acts. This develops creation and responsibility: the moment of birth is the moment of abandonment.
Imagery
Plot

Guilt imagined as hell. The evidence is “I was seized by remorse and the sense of guilt, which hurried me away to a hell of intense tortures” (Chapter IX, paragraph 1). This develops the sublime: nature offers temporary relief from guilt. The words “tortures” and “remorse” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Human violence comes first. The evidence is “some fled, some attacked me” (Chapter XI, paragraph 10). This develops nature and nurture: he begins innocent; humans attack him on sight. The words “attacked” and “fled” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

A question of identity. The evidence is “And what was I” (Chapter XIII, paragraph 17). This develops ambition and knowledge: "Of what a strange nature is knowledge!": knowledge as a burden. The words “what” and “was” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
Chapter XIII
Chapter XV

After he saves a girl and is shot, he asks bitterly whether "this was then the reward of my benevolence," and soon he bears "a hell within me"; the novel traces how injustice breeds hatred while still making him kill William by his own will. The evidence is “This was then the reward of my benevolence” (Chapter XVI, paragraph 20) — Shot after a rescue; bitter irony. This develops nature and nurture: repeated cruelty turns his benevolence into vengeance.

He asks whether his "murderous machinations" have killed Henry, naming his own schemes as the cause. The evidence is “Have my murderous machinations deprived you also, my dearest Henry, of life” (Chapter XXI, paragraph 9) — Self-blame. This develops creation and responsibility: Victor calls himself the cause.

Repetition of the threat. The evidence is “I shall be with you on your wedding night” (Chapter XXII, paragraph 29). This develops isolation and companionship: secrets poison his relationship with Elizabeth. The words “wedding” and “night” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

He confesses only in riddles ("I am the assassin") and fixates on the creature's threat to himself, so the one person who loves him never learns the danger she is in. The evidence is “I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations” (Chapter XXII, paragraph 6) — Confession to his father, dismissed as madness. This develops isolation and companionship: secrets poison his relationship with Elizabeth.
Imagery
Structure

The stated moral purpose. Students can test whether the plot actually shows this, or shows what happens when domestic affection is withheld. The evidence is “the amiableness of domestic affection, and the excellence of universal virtue” (Preface, paragraph 3). This develops creation and responsibility: The Preface claims the story shows "the amiableness of domestic affection"; keep this phrase on the board. The novel will test it: domestic love is shown, then destroyed. The words “amiableness” and “excellence” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. By citing Dr. Darwin and German physiologists it claims the event is "not of impossible occurrence," and by naming domestic affection and virtue as its aims it answers the charge that a horror story is immoral.

"Satiate" (fully satisfy) and "ardent" reveal appetite-like ambition. Use for a claim about the dangers of curiosity. The evidence is “I shall satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited” (Letter I, paragraph 2). This develops ambition and knowledge: Walton dreams of "a part of the world never before visited." The novel begins with a second Victor before we meet the first. The words “curiosity” and “visited” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. His dream of a land "never before visited" and his heart that glows with enthusiasm use the same fevered vocabulary Victor will use about creating life, which invites readers to compare the two men.

The creature will ask for exactly this. Evidence that the need for companionship is universal in the novel. The evidence is “I desire the company of a man who could sympathise with me; whose eyes would reply to mine” (Letter II, paragraph 2). This develops isolation and companionship: the desire for a sympathetic friend is the thread connecting Walton, Victor and the creature. The words “sympathise” and “company” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. His wish for someone whose "eyes would reply to mine" names the sympathy every major character lacks, so the novel ties ambition to isolation from its first pages.

A rhetorical question the novel answers: nature, death and conscience can. The evidence is “What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man” (Letter III, paragraph 4). This develops ambition and knowledge: the "determined heart and resolved will of man" sounds heroic but is the attitude the novel interrogates. The words “determined” and “resolved” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Asking "What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?" assumes nothing can; the rest of the book, beginning with the ice that traps his ship, shows that something always does.

(The 1831 text prints "drank.") Victor calls ambition a drug ("intoxicating draught") and madness. Evidence for the novel's view of obsessive curiosity. The evidence is “Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you drank also of the intoxicating draught” (Letter IV, paragraph 25). This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor recognizes himself in Walton and warns him; the story becomes a cautionary tale told for a listener's benefit. The words “intoxicating” and “madness” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. By calling Walton's desire an "intoxicating draught" and hoping it will not be "a serpent to sting you," Victor links the pursuit of knowledge to addiction and to the biblical Fall, so everything he tells next is offered as a lesson.

Waldman's contrast between old and modern science. The evidence is “promised impossibilities, and performed nothing” (Chapter III, paragraph 16). This develops ambition and knowledge: Waldman says modern scientists "penetrate into the recesses of nature"; Victor answers with a vow to go further. The words “impossibilities” and “performed” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Right after his mother's death he hears Waldman praise modern science and vows "more, far more, will I achieve," showing ambition rushing to fill the space left by loss.

The novel's warning stated outright. The evidence is “Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge” (Chapter IV, paragraph 6). This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor fantasizes that "a new species would bless me as its creator," revealing the wish to be worshipped. The words “acquirement” and “dangerous” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He imagines a new species that "would bless me as its creator," which centers his own glory; nothing in his plans considers what the being will need.

The turn from ambition to revulsion in one sentence. The evidence is “the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart” (Chapter V, paragraph 3). This develops creation and responsibility: the moment of birth is the moment of abandonment. The words “breathless” and “vanished” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The creature's "hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me," a gesture of need, and Victor simply "escaped"; the word "seemingly" shows he does not know what it wants and does not stay to find out.

Victor concludes guilt from appearance, as others will judge the creature. The evidence is “Nothing in human shape could have destroyed that fair child” (Chapter VII, paragraph 29). This develops creation and responsibility: the first death caused (indirectly) by Victor's creation. The words “destroyed” and “child” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He decides that "nothing in human shape could have destroyed that fair child," so he is certain who did it, yet he lets Justine be accused rather than reveal his secret.

Psychological insight into grief and guilt. The evidence is “Nothing is more painful to the human mind, than, after the feelings have been worked up by a quick succession of events, the dead calmness…” (Chapter IX, paragraph 1). This develops the sublime: nature offers temporary relief from guilt. The words “succession” and “certainty” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He describes "the dead calmness of inaction and certainty" as the most painful state of mind, and his remorse becomes "a hell of intense tortures"; suffering replaces confession, so guilt leads nowhere.

Benevolence repaid with treachery. The evidence is “The father of Safie had been the cause of their ruin” (Chapter XIV, paragraph 3). This develops isolation and companionship: the De Laceys, poor and exiled, still have each other; the creature has no one. The words “father” and “cause” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The family's ruin comes from helping the man whose daughter Felix loves, since "the father of Safie had been the cause of their ruin"; goodness here is no protection.

Anguish and accusation. The evidence is “Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live” (Chapter XVI, paragraph 1). This develops nature and nurture: repeated cruelty turns his benevolence into vengeance. The words “creator” and “cursed” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. After he saves a girl and is shot, he asks bitterly whether "this was then the reward of my benevolence," and soon he bears "a hell within me"; the novel traces how injustice breeds hatred while still making him kill William by his own will.

Milton's Satan: the hell is internal. The evidence is “I, like the archfiend, bore a hell within me” (Chapter XVI, paragraph 2). This develops nature and nurture: repeated cruelty turns his benevolence into vengeance. The words “archfiend” and “within” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. After he saves a girl and is shot, he asks bitterly whether "this was then the reward of my benevolence," and soon he bears "a hell within me"; the novel traces how injustice breeds hatred while still making him kill William by his own will.

Fear and disgust pull against each other: the source of his delay. The evidence is “I feared the vengeance of the disappointed fiend, yet I was unable to overcome my repugnance to the task which was enjoined me” (Chapter XVIII, paragraph 1). This develops isolation and companionship: Victor feels "an insurmountable barrier" between himself and others. The words “disappointed” and “repugnance” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He fears "the vengeance of the disappointed fiend" but cannot overcome his "repugnance to the task," and so he drifts; by his own admission he becomes "the slave of my creature.".

Revulsion at his labor. The evidence is “my heart often sickened at the work of my hands” (Chapter XIX, paragraph 21). This develops creation and responsibility: making a second being makes him think about consequences, at last. The words “sickened” and “hands” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He says his "heart often sickened at the work of my hands," a sharp contrast to the rapture of the first creation, which shows responsibility arriving too late.

Mocking accusation. The evidence is “with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife” (Chapter XXIII, paragraph 10). This develops creation and responsibility: Victor becomes the pursuer. The words “fiendish” and “pointed” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He says "a fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness," the same hopeless isolation the creature described, and like the creature he turns to vengeance.

Victor's lesson; partly retracted. The evidence is “Seek happiness in tranquillity, and avoid ambition” (Chapter XXIV, paragraph 57). This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor's final advice: "Seek happiness in tranquillity and avoid ambition.". The words “tranquillity” and “happiness” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Victor advises "seek happiness in tranquillity and avoid ambition" yet adds that another may succeed; the creature disappears into "darkness and distance," leaving judgment open.

This develops ambition and knowledge: the desire to learn "the secrets of heaven and earth" begins as wonder and becomes obsession. Calling natural philosophy "the genius that has regulated my fate" makes science an outside force, and he blames his father's careless "sad trash" for not stopping him; readers can see a man explaining away his own will.

The novel's warning stated outright. The evidence is “Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge” (Chapter IV, paragraph 6). This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor fantasizes that "a new species would bless me as its creator," revealing the wish to be worshipped. The words “acquirement” and “dangerous” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He imagines a new species that "would bless me as its creator," which centers his own glory; nothing in his plans considers what the being will need.

Pathetic fallacy and anticlimax: "accomplishment" is followed by horror. The evidence is “It was on a dreary night of November, that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils” (Chapter V, paragraph 1). This develops creation and responsibility: the moment of birth is the moment of abandonment. The words “accomplishment” and “beheld” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The creature's "hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me," a gesture of need, and Victor simply "escaped"; the word "seemingly" shows he does not know what it wants and does not stay to find out.

The turn from ambition to revulsion in one sentence. The evidence is “the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart” (Chapter V, paragraph 3). This develops creation and responsibility: the moment of birth is the moment of abandonment. The words “breathless” and “vanished” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The creature's "hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me," a gesture of need, and Victor simply "escaped"; the word "seemingly" shows he does not know what it wants and does not stay to find out.

Restoration that the reader suspects cannot last. The evidence is “I became the same happy creature who, a few years ago, loved and beloved by all, had no sorrow or care” (Chapter VI, paragraph 21). This develops isolation and companionship: Clerval shows what companionship gives: Victor says a selfish pursuit had "cramped and narrowed" him. The words “creature” and “beloved” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Victor credits Clerval's "gentleness and affection" for curing what a "selfish pursuit" had done, so he knows what care is; he has simply not given it to his creation.

Victor makes Justine's death about his suffering: a striking self-centeredness. The evidence is “The tortures of the accused did not equal mine” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 11). This develops creation and responsibility: guilt without action: Victor feels remorse but does not act. The words “tortures” and “accused” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He claims "the tortures of the accused did not equal mine," even though she is the one executed, so his remorse becomes another form of self-focus rather than action.

Elizabeth sees what Victor hides; his guilt shows on his face. The evidence is “There is an expression of despair, and sometimes of revenge, in your countenance, that makes me tremble” (Chapter IX, paragraph 9). This develops the sublime: nature offers temporary relief from guilt. The words “countenance” and “expression” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He describes "the dead calmness of inaction and certainty" as the most painful state of mind, and his remorse becomes "a hell of intense tortures"; suffering replaces confession, so guilt leads nowhere.

Self-horror learned from others' standards of beauty. The evidence is “how was I terrified, when I viewed myself in a transparent pool” (Chapter XII, paragraph 13). This develops nature and nurture: he learns virtue by watching virtue. The words “transparent” and “terrified” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. When he realizes that stealing "inflicted pain on the cottagers," he "abstained," choosing others' welfare over his own hunger without being taught.

Isolation through allusion. The evidence is “Like Adam, I was apparently united by no link to any other being in existence” (Chapter XV, paragraph 7). This develops nature and nurture: rejection is based on sight; the blind man alone judges him by his words. The words “apparently” and “existence” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Old De Lacey, who is blind, responds kindly to his words, but the family sees him and attacks; the scene shows that only someone who cannot see him can judge him fairly.

Milton's Satan: the hell is internal. The evidence is “I, like the archfiend, bore a hell within me” (Chapter XVI, paragraph 2). This develops nature and nurture: repeated cruelty turns his benevolence into vengeance. The words “archfiend” and “within” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. After he saves a girl and is shot, he asks bitterly whether "this was then the reward of my benevolence," and soon he bears "a hell within me"; the novel traces how injustice breeds hatred while still making him kill William by his own will.

Anguish and accusation. The evidence is “Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live” (Chapter XVI, paragraph 1). This develops nature and nurture: repeated cruelty turns his benevolence into vengeance. The words “creator” and “cursed” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. After he saves a girl and is shot, he asks bitterly whether "this was then the reward of my benevolence," and soon he bears "a hell within me"; the novel traces how injustice breeds hatred while still making him kill William by his own will.

The argument from isolation. The evidence is “If I have no ties and no affections, hatred and vice must be my portion” (Chapter XVII, paragraph 14). This develops isolation and companionship: the plea for a companion is the novel's most direct statement of the need for love. The words “affections” and “portion” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He calls sympathy "necessary for my being" and warns that without "ties" and "affections" he must turn to "hatred and vice," linking moral life to belonging.

Victor's fear of consequences. The evidence is “a race of devils would be propagated upon the earth” (Chapter XX, paragraph 2). This develops creation and responsibility: is destroying the female responsible or another betrayal?. The words “propagated” and “devils” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He fears "a race of devils would be propagated upon the earth," thinking of future people, yet he does it in front of the creature, who answers "I shall be with you on your wedding-night.".

Victor's grief and guilt break his body and he falls into a long illness. The evidence is “The human frame could no longer support the agonies that I endured” (Chapter XXI, paragraph 10). This develops creation and responsibility: Victor calls himself the cause. The words “support” and “endured” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He asks whether his "murderous machinations" have killed Henry, naming his own schemes as the cause.

Echoes the "lifeless matter" of creation. The evidence is “She was there, lifeless and inanimate, thrown across the bed” (Chapter XXIII, paragraph 8). This develops creation and responsibility: Victor becomes the pursuer. The words “inanimate” and “lifeless” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He says "a fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness," the same hopeless isolation the creature described, and like the creature he turns to vengeance.

Mocking accusation. The evidence is “with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife” (Chapter XXIII, paragraph 10). This develops creation and responsibility: Victor becomes the pursuer. The words “fiendish” and “pointed” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He says "a fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness," the same hopeless isolation the creature described, and like the creature he turns to vengeance.

finalPaper.title: Frankenstein: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition across Frankenstein. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Frankenstein and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to creation and responsibility.
Analyze a central character's choices in Frankenstein. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether Frankenstein finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of isolation and the need for companionship. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: Shelley frames her novel as a creation that, unlike Victor's, is accepted and sent out with care. The text makes this visible when it says “And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper” (Introduction, paragraph 15). By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.

criticalVoices.quote: Frightful must it be; for supremely frightful would be the effect of any human endeavour to mock the stupendous mechanism of the Creator of the world.
criticalVoices.speaker: Mary Shelley, author (Introduction to the revised edition, 1831)
criticalVoices.source: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (London: Colburn and Bentley, 1831), Author's Introduction, Introduction, the waking-dream paragraph
criticalVoices.useNote: Thesis test: does the 1831 author frame ambition as blasphemy, and does the 1818 novel itself make that judgment? Students weigh the author's later frame against Walton's last letters (outside source for HS Senior and up; this introduction is not in the 1818 text).

criticalVoices.quote: Nor are the crimes and malevolence of the single Being, though indeed withering and tremendous, the offspring of any unaccountable propensity to evil, but flow irresistibly from certain causes fully adequate to their production. They are the children, as it were, of Necessity and Human Nature.

criticalVoices.useNote: Counter-argument starter: use Shelley as the "society made him" reading, then answer the strongest objection (the murders of William and Elizabeth) from the Creature's own words in the last chapter.
